newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore, Britain sign taxation agreement.
newsitem.headline: Singapore, Britain sign taxation agreement.

text.p: Singapore and Britain on Wednesday signed an agreement avoiding double taxation, Singapore's finance ministry said.

Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu and British Foreign Secretary Malcom Rifkind signed the pact ahead of Thursday's ministerial meetings between Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the European Union.
The two-day ASEAN-EU meetings will be followed by the Asia-Europe Foreign Ministers' meeting on Saturday.
The agreement will replace one signed on December 1, 1966, and amended by a protocol signed on July 21, 1975.
"The old agreement has worked well for both countries but changes in economic circumstances and policies since 1975 have made it necessary to review and revise it," the statement said.
Among changes under the new agreement, the rates of withholding tax on interest and royalties will be reduced below those in the old agreement to 10 percent from January 1, 2000.
The British tax treatment of British dividends derived by a Singapore resident will also differ from the old agreement.

Singapore resident companies controlling less than 10 percent of the voting power of a British company and Singapore residents will no longer be allowed to claim a credit of the Advance Corporation Tax on the dividends.
The credit is currently 25 percent of gross dividends.
The new agreement will also impact Singapore's ability to compete for foreign investment from Britain.
This is due to the gradual removal of the tax sparing credit which Britain grants under the old agreement.
The ministry said the new agreement would avoid the burden of double taxation between Singapore and Britain.
It will come into effect after it has been ratified by both countries.
